sources.title: Compatibility of Concurrent Aerobic and Strength Training for Skeletal Muscle Size and Function: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Schumann M et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 43 controlled studies; healthy adults; supervised concurrent training >=4 weeks vs identical strength alone. Chronic strength, explosive strength and hypertrophy, not next-morning readiness.
sources.findings: Pooled maximal strength and hypertrophy did not show clear attenuation; explosive-strength attenuation was present, especially close/session combinations. No universal compatibility or spacing claim follows.
sources.locator: Abstract Methods/Results; Discussion sections on explosive strength and limitations; publisher lines185-214.
limitations: Mostly medium/low methodological quality; intensity not consistently reported
Active training status pooled broadly; chronic group estimates cannot identify acute individual adequacy
counterevidence: L04 finds endpoint/subgroup attenuation under different definitions
No order-specific pooled effect established here; same-session power exception matters

sources.title: Acute Neuromuscular, Physiological and Performance Responses After Strength Training in Runners: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: de Carvalho e Silva GI et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 19 qualitative/13 meta-analyzed studies of runners after resistance exercise; heterogeneous strength protocols, tasks and assessment times.
sources.findings: Acute peak torque and subjective/muscle-damage measures could worsen while several submaximal running physiological outcomes showed little change. Task and dose matter.
sources.locator: Results; Discussion including protocol contrasts; limitations and practical implications, publisher lines198-211.
limitations: Too few studies for robust 6/10/24/48h recovery curve
Does not quantify cost of the exact squat/RDL/split or guarantee a reduced set restores performance
counterevidence: Some submaximal tasks not impaired; reducing every lower/run pairing is unjustified
No single protocol result can define all runners time-to-recovery

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.authors: Currier BS et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 137 systematic reviews of randomized healthy-adult RT interventions,6-52 weeks; literature search October2024. General strength, hypertrophy, function and power outcomes.
sources.findings: Progressive RT with goal-specific variables is supported; many configurations work. Failure is not necessary; exact optimal set counts and individual response cannot be read from pooled summaries.
sources.locator: Eligibility; Tables3/6; Discussion and limitations lines900-924. Full text newly available in this round, unlike pilot abstract access.
limitations: Review overlap quantified only for strength; variable-level overview not comparison of all compound programs
Group-level general adult evidence does not certify an individual dose, clinical clearance, or specialized concurrent/taper program
counterevidence: More volume may improve some outcomes; omitted work is not assumed equivalent
Specificity and goal change can make a convenient substitute inadequate

sources.title: Concurrent Strength and Endurance Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on the Impact of Sex and Training Status
sources.authors: Huiberts RO, Wust RCI, van der Zwaard S
sources.population_design_dose: 59 studies/1346 healthy adults18-50, concurrent >=4 weeks; strength/endurance training status classified separately. Online2023, issue2024.
sources.findings: Subgroup and outcome-specific attenuation qualifies universal no-interference claims. Highly strength-trained populations were absent; female hypertrophy data sparse.
sources.locator: Methods2.2-2.6; Results3.1/3.4/3.5; Discussion.
limitations: Mostly untrained strength participants; limited highly trained endurance evidence
Subgroup association does not select acute action from sex or prove female safety
counterevidence: Different definitions and endpoints fromL01; no vote-counting or same-PICO contradiction invented
Not an individual prediction or automatic priority policy

sources.title: Monitoring the athlete training response: subjective self-reported measures trump commonly used objective measures: a systematic review
sources.authors: Saw AE, Main LC, Gastin PB
sources.population_design_dose: Systematic descriptive synthesis of 56 studies in training athletes; established self-report instruments compared with concurrent objective measures. Competition periods excluded.
sources.findings: Subjective well-being was responsive to training changes; subjective and objective measures were not consistently associated. Supports monitoring, not a validated decision algorithm.
sources.locator: Methods: selection, extraction, descriptive synthesis; Results/Tables 6-7; Practical considerations and Limitations, PMC lines 106-195, 361-422, 519-545.
limitations: Search through May 2014; heterogeneous timeframes and sampling; small samples and selective reporting.
Review excluded sRPE as well-being; bespoke single-item product questions are not automatically equivalent to validated instruments.
counterevidence: Total scores can dilute subscale changes; biomarker disagreement is possible.
No universal readiness cutoff, reduction dose or clinical diagnosis established.

sources.title: Monitoring Training Load to Understand Fatigue in Athletes
sources.authors: Halson SL
sources.population_design_dose: Narrative review of practical athlete load/fatigue monitoring; includes elite-context examples, not an intervention trial.
sources.findings: No single definitive fatigue marker; internal/external load, protocol, context and individual longitudinal response need interpretation together.
sources.locator: Internal versus External Load; Methods6.1-6.13; questionnaires and sleep.
limitations: Narrative contextual source, ineligible as decisive prescriptive support
Some examples/technologies are older; not a proposed product biomarker algorithm
counterevidence: RPE/HR/HRV affected by protocol and environment
No guarantee monitoring improves performance or identifies clinical risk

sources.title: The Effect of Load and Volume Autoregulation on Muscular Strength and Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Hickmott LM, Chilibeck PD, Shaw KA, Butcher SJ
sources.population_design_dose: 15 studies:6 load-autoregulation and9 volume-autoregulation; resistance-trained populations, chronic1RM and muscle CSA outcomes.
sources.findings: Autoregulated versus standardized load produced similar strength gains overall; volume/protocol endpoints varied. RIR-based estimates are subjective and can be inaccurate.
sources.locator: Results/Discussion, load and volume prescription; Primary Limitations, publisher lines247-257 and308 onward.
limitations: No universal superiority of autoregulation
Velocity-loss bins not transferable to a numerical RIR/reps progression cutoff
Does not validate the exact4-6rep/2-4RIR/2.5kg fixture envelope
counterevidence: NewerL11 abstract reaches broader superiority wording; inaccessible full methods and protocol mixtures prevent upgrading to universal claim
Preauthorized execution flexibility and target mutation are distinct product decisions

sources.title: Does Taking a Break Matter—Adaptations in Muscle Strength and Size Between Continuous and Periodic Resistance Training
sources.authors: Halonen EJ, Gabriel I, Kelahaara MM, Ahtiainen JP, Hulmi JJ
sources.population_design_dose: 55 initially eligible untrained18-40 males/females; physician health inclusion; periodic10wkRT/10wkbreak/10wkretraining vs continuous20wkRT; machine leg press and biceps curl outcomes.
sources.findings: Strength and size recovered during retraining after detraining; no statistically significant between-group difference in final studied adaptations was detected. This is not proof of equivalence and does not test catch-up volume.
sources.locator: Methods2.1/2.2; Results3.2; Discussion4.1/4.2.
limitations: Not trained concurrent runners or exact14 day pause; no restart load/volume percentage derived
Physician-screened research inclusion is not software eligibility clearance
Authors explicitly exclude applying findings to illness/injury interruptions
counterevidence: Detraining caused changes before regain; no presumption old targets remain appropriate
Specific machine/untrained outcomes do not prove barbell or running reentry dose

sources.title: Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Wang Z, Wang YT, Gao W, Zhong Y
sources.population_design_dose: 14 studies/174 athletes17-32; mainly male running/cycling; well-trained or VO2max>55 inclusion. Controlled taper trials with varied doses/durations.
sources.findings: Tapering can improve endurance time-trial outcomes; moderator estimates are not a universal taper recipe. Competition-specific and concurrent-strength doses remain individual questions.
sources.locator: Eligibility criteria; Table1; Results/Table2; Limitations and conclusion.
limitations: FewRCTs; mostly men; limited training-status comparison
Specialized well-trained endurance evidence not all recreational adults
No exact combined10 kmstrength taper validated
counterevidence: Some moderators inconsistent; no universal41-60% reduction or<=21day command
Race cancellation/postponement changes intent, not automatic restoration of old workload

sources.title: Maximizing Adaptations in Concurrent Training: An Umbrella Review of Meta-analyses
sources.authors: Held S et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 17meta-analyses, 144individual studies,1492participants as reported in publisher abstract; search February2025; subscription preview.
sources.findings: Broad concurrent-training compatibility is reported; abstract acknowledges sparse highly trained/elite evidence. Used for currency/countercontext only.
sources.locator: Publisher Abstract and explicit subscription-preview label lines44-62.
limitations: Full methods/results inaccessible; not sole prescriptive support
Underlying reviews overlap; not independent replication ofL01/L04
counterevidence: Does not override endpoint-specific power or acute task findings
Abstract sequence wording cannot prove a universally preferred order

sources.title: Autoregulated resistance training for maximal strength enhancement: A systematic review and network meta-analysis
sources.authors: Huang Z et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Networkmeta-analysis of APRE/RPE/velocity/percentage-based training; abstract and indexed selected text; PMC challenge and publisher403 blocked fulltext.
sources.findings: Authors favor autoregulated methods overall; protocol/endpoint ranking differs and abstract intervals do not support a universal superiority rule.
sources.locator: PubMed Abstract Results/Conclusions; fulltext not read.
limitations: Full-text access missing in this instance
Indirect comparisons and protocol mixtures require full-method appraisal
counterevidence: L07 did not show general load-autoregulation superiority
Neither source validates exact fixture progression thresholds

sources.title: Effect of Strength Training Programs in Middle- and Long-Distance Runners' Economy at Different Running Speeds: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis
sources.authors: Llanos-Lagos C, Ramirez-Campillo R, Moran J, Sáez de Villarreal E
sources.population_design_dose: Moderately to highly trained runners; strength interventions 6-24 weeks, 1-4 sessions/week. Economy assessed at heterogeneous speeds.
sources.findings: Heavy-load, plyometric and combined methods can improve economy; magnitude and applicability depend on tested method, speed and population.
sources.locator: Methods 2.3-2.4; Results 3.5; Discussion 4.1-4.3 and Conclusions.
limitations: Sparse female/highly trained subgroup evidence; mostly absolute testing speeds.
Economy outcome does not prove injury prevention or exact session necessity.
counterevidence: Submaximal/isometric methods had no significant main improvement; not proof of ineffectiveness for every goal.
Benefits of chronic training coexist with L02 acute burden.

sources.title: Which Training Intensity Distribution Intervention will Produce the Greatest Improvements in Maximal Oxygen Uptake and Time-Trial Performance in Endurance Athletes? A Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis of Individual Participant Data
sources.authors: Rosenblat MA et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 13 studies, 348 trained endurance athletes across sports; 296 men/52 women. Abstract; search through February 2024.
sources.findings: No statistically significant overall POL-PYR difference reported for VO2max or time trial; performance-level subgroup results differ.
sources.locator: Publisher Abstract Methods/Results, lines 50-68; explicit subscription preview.
limitations: Full methods/results unavailable; auxiliary only.
Mixed sports; overlapping trials with L19.
counterevidence: Does not justify universal POL superiority or universal recreational PYR prescription.
No significant difference is not equivalence.

sources.title: Heart Rate Variability-Guided Training for Enhancing Cardiac-Vagal Modulation, Aerobic Fitness, and Endurance Performance: A Methodological Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Manresa-Rocamora A, Sarabia JM, Javaloyes A, Flatt AA, Moya-Ramón M
sources.population_design_dose: Healthy sedentary to endurance-trained adults; HRV-guided versus predefined programs; abstract and discovery excerpts only.
sources.findings: Small uncertain fitness/performance advantages reported; HRV methods and reference values require further study.
sources.locator: PubMed Abstract Methods/Results/Conclusion; PMC challenge and publisher 429 prevented full-text appraisal.
limitations: Not sole prescriptive support; no autonomous HRV algorithm validated.
Overlaps Düking 2021 and earlier HRV reviews.
counterevidence: A changed HRV value does not itself decide a plan mutation.
No significant group advantage does not prove equivalence.

sources.title: A Systematic Review Examining the Approaches Used to Estimate Interindividual Differences in Trainability and Classify Individual Responses to Exercise Training
sources.authors: Bonafiglia JT, Preobrazenski N, Gurd BJ
sources.population_design_dose: 149 studies across aerobic, resistance and clinical literature; methodological review, not an athlete coaching trial.
sources.findings: Observed response variation cannot automatically be attributed to trainability; measurement error, within-person variation and meaningful change require consideration.
sources.locator: Methods classification; Results/Table 3; Discussion and Limitations, publisher lines 455-573.
limitations: Mixed outcomes/populations; most studies had unclear-high risk of bias.
Does not validate a personalization algorithm or required observation count.
counterevidence: Few studies tested response-guided later prescription; stable responder labels can mislead.
Better observation does not establish causal lower-before-run intolerance.

sources.title: The accuracy of fixed intensity anchors to estimate lactate thresholds in recreational runners
sources.authors: Nuuttila O-P, Kaikkonen P, Sievänen H, Vasankari T, Kyröläinen H
sources.population_design_dose: Pooled baseline treadmill tests in 165 recreational runners (64 women/101 men), accustomed to running; incremental lactate measurements.
sources.findings: Fixed relative anchors have individual error; estimated maximal values worsened accuracy. RPE was the least accurate tested threshold estimator.
sources.locator: Methods Participants/Incremental test/Lactate assessment; Results Tables 3-5; Discussion, publisher lines 97-176.
limitations: Cross-sectional laboratory association, not chronic prescription trial.
Specific lactate method/protocol; cannot certify field thresholds or universal sex rules.
counterevidence: RPE remains usable for effort intent; it cannot be renamed a measured physiological threshold.
Measured maxima reduce some error but do not eliminate individual uncertainty.

sources.title: How much running is too much? Identifying high-risk running sessions in a 5200-person cohort study
sources.authors: Frandsen JSB et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 18-month observational cohort, 5205 adult Garmin users, mean age 45.8 years, 22% women; self-reported overuse injury.
sources.findings: Single-session distance spikes relative to recent longest run were associated with injury; no week-to-week association reported.
sources.locator: PubMed abstract Methods/Results; PMC header initially accessible, later challenge; full methods/limitations not appraised.
limitations: Observational association; self-report and selection/confounding require full-text appraisal.
Not sole prescriptive support or a validated injury forecast.
counterevidence: Does not validate a universally safe 10% increase.
Session-distance exposure differs from weekly progression and ignores strength dose.

sources.title: Prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of the overtraining syndrome: joint consensus statement of the European College of Sport Science and the American College of Sports Medicine
sources.authors: Meeusen R, Duclos M, Foster C, Fry A, Gleeson M, Nieman D, Raglin J, Rietjens G, Steinacker J, Urhausen A
sources.population_design_dose: Consensus on overtraining/overreaching and exclusion diagnosis; no product or individual assessment.
sources.findings: No single accepted diagnostic marker; persistent maladaptation requires differential assessment beyond routine fatigue adjustment.
sources.locator: PubMed abstract; full consensus not read in this instance.
limitations: Historical and abstract-only; auxiliary boundary context.
No software diagnosis, biomarker clearance or recovery-day count supported.
counterevidence: Short performance decrement alone is not OTS.
Prolonged unexplained decline cannot be relabeled benign fatigue.

sources.title: Comparison of Polarized Versus Other Types of Endurance Training Intensity Distribution on Athletes' Endurance Performance: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis
sources.authors: Silva Oliveira P, Boppre G, Fonseca H
sources.population_design_dose: 17 controlled studies, 437 participants; >=4 weeks, >=3 endurance sessions/week; mixed sports/training levels.
sources.findings: Small VO2peak advantage for POL; other performance endpoints did not show superiority. Training level and duration were entangled.
sources.locator: Methods 2.1-2.3; Results; Discussion and limitations lines 295-308.
limitations: Some actual intensity distributions and program variables underreported.
Not direct hybrid-plan optimization; overlap with L13.
counterevidence: Cannot infer universal 80/20 ratio or novice applicability.
Null endpoint differences are not equivalence.

sources.title: No effect of a graded training program on the number of running-related injuries in novice runners: a randomized controlled trial
sources.authors: Buist I, Bredeweg SW, van Mechelen W, Lemmink KAPM, Pepping G-J, Diercks RL
sources.population_design_dose: 532 novice runners preparing for 4 miles; 13-week 10%-rule program versus standard 8-week program.
sources.findings: No significant preventive effect detected for the graded program on running-related injury.
sources.locator: PubMed Abstract Methods/Results/Conclusions; protocol is a separate paper and not outcome evidence.
limitations: Abstract-only; auxiliary counterevidence.
Different durations and complete programs, not isolated percentage comparison.
counterevidence: Does not establish equivalent injury risk or show that faster progression is safe.
Refutes assuming a 10%-rule injury-prevention guarantee.

sources.title: Effects of Short-Term Concurrent Training Cessation on the Energy Cost of Running and Neuromuscular Performances in Middle-Distance Runners
sources.authors: Berryman N, Mujika I, Bosquet L
sources.population_design_dose: Descriptive follow-up: 8 well-trained male runners novice to strength; 8 weeks combined training, then 4 weeks strength cessation while running continued; no completing control.
sources.findings: Economy benefits were largely maintained in the small follow-up; individual deterioration also occurred.
sources.locator: Methods 2.1-2.4; Results 3; Discussion 4, PMC lines 104-111, 147-204.
limitations: High dropout selection, n=8 and no control; weak auxiliary evidence.
Strength-only interruption is not whole-training cessation.
counterevidence: Does not validate combined taper dose or automatic full strength removal.
Cannot prescribe exact re-entry after a nonclinical pause.

sources.title: Impact of weekly frequency of high-intensity interval training on cardiorespiratory, metabolic, and performance measures in recreational runners – An exploratory study
sources.authors: Lenk M, Matzka M, Lauber L, Kunz P, Sperlich B
sources.population_design_dose: 26 of 44 young recreationally active participants completed; randomly assigned 1/2/3 weekly 4x4-min sessions for 6 weeks; baseline-calibrated treadmill targets and 3-min active rest.
sources.findings: Provides a concrete studied interval structure; exploratory outcomes do not establish a universally optimal frequency.
sources.locator: Methods 2.1-2.5; Results/Table 1; Discussion 4.1, PMC lines 111-179, 203-211.
limitations: Small samples, high attrition, no a priori power; imprecise effects and no significant frequency interaction.
Not novice or concurrent-program dose validation.
counterevidence: No significant between-group difference does not justify prescribing 2-3 HIIT sessions/week universally.
Tested fixed anchors still require L16 calibration caveats.

sources.title: Run Clever - No difference in risk of injury when comparing progression in running volume and running intensity in recreational runners: A randomised trial
sources.authors: Ramskov D, Rasmussen S, Sørensen H, Parner ET, Lind M, Nielsen RO
sources.population_design_dose: 839 initially enrolled healthy recreational runners; 447 after 8-week preconditioning entered 16-week intensity- versus volume-focus progression.
sources.findings: No significant difference in injury proportion detected; broad risk-difference intervals allow important uncertainty.
sources.locator: PubMed Abstract Methods/Results; PMC challenge/BMJ403 in this instance.
limitations: Not direct novice-program dose evidence or equivalence.
Preconditioning attrition; no full-method appraisal here.
counterevidence: Related Run Clever injury reports are overlapping participants, not independent trials.
No universal preference for intensity- or volume-first progression established.

sources.title: The Measurement and Application of Critical Speed and D′ in Running: A Scoping Review
sources.authors: Anderson M, Sabapathy S, Arnold B, Bellenger C, Kolodziej F, Bellinger P
sources.population_design_dose: Scoping review with systematic search through December 2025; running CS/D-prime measurement, modelling and training application. Not effectiveness meta-analysis.
sources.findings: Protocol/model choices affect estimates; CS and other threshold estimates cannot be used interchangeably. Longitudinal D-prime-balance training evidence is absent in the review.
sources.locator: Methods 2.1-2.3; Results 3.1/3.3; Discussion 4.1/4.3; Crossmark current on accessed record.
limitations: Descriptive scoping design; abstract/full-text study counts differ (124/132), not resolved here.
Field/environment variation and D-prime reconstitution uncertainty remain.
counterevidence: Same percent of CS can impose different cost across athletes.
No universal interval or exact threshold dose derived.

stopping_reason: Decision-relevant frameworks and limits identified; additional generic studies would not determine individual dose, safe progression, combined taper or exact re-entry. Owned gaps retained.
